text:
**The Case for the Joined-Up Line**

Every few years, someone declares handwriting dead. The keyboard has won, the argument goes, so why spend precious classroom hours teaching seven-year-olds to loop an "l" into an "e"? Finland stopped requiring cursive in 2016. Several American states dropped it from their standards, and some later reversed course. Teachers are overstretched, the curriculum is crowded, and a child who will one day type for a living does not obviously need a flowing hand. It is a tidy argument, and I think it is wrong. Primary schools should keep teaching joined-up handwriting, and they should teach it well.

Start with what the case against it gets right, because it gets some things right. Handwriting is not sacred. Nobody should be marked down for a lazy "g", and no child should be humiliated for untidy work. Typing is a necessary skill, and children who cannot touch-type by the end of primary school are at a real disadvantage in secondary school. If the choice were between teaching keyboarding and teaching cursive, and nothing else were at stake, keyboarding might win. But that is not the choice. Schools can do both, and the evidence suggests that dropping handwriting costs more than it saves.

The strongest reason is cognitive. When a child writes by hand, she has to produce each letter from memory, shaping it with her own movements. When she types, she only has to find it on a keyboard. That difference matters. Studies by researchers such as Karin James, using brain imaging, found that young children who practised letters by hand showed richer activation in the regions linked to reading than those who typed or traced them. A 2014 paper by Pam Mueller and Daniel Oppenheimer found that students who took notes longhand tended to understand the material better than laptop users, partly because they could not transcribe everything and so had to think about what mattered. Some of these findings have been challenged, and the notetaking result has had mixed replications. I do not want to oversell any single study. Still, the broad direction is consistent. Handwriting is not just a way of recording thought. It helps build it.

Why joined-up in particular, rather than print? Here the case is less about neuroscience and more about the practical mechanics of writing. A cursive hand, or even a semi-joined one, lets the pen stay on the page. Letters flow into one another, and words become single motions rather than strings of separate stabs. For many children this makes writing faster and less tiring. It also removes one of the commonest errors of early writing, which is the confusion of letters that differ only by orientation. A child who prints "b" and "d" as lollipops on opposite sides of a stick may reverse them for years. A child who learns each from a joining entry stroke tends to find them far more distinct. Teachers of children with dyslexia have recommended cursive for exactly this reason for decades, and the Dyslexia Association and similar bodies have generally supported it. It is not a magic fix, but it is a genuinely useful one.

Speed matters more than people assume. Pupils sit exams by hand. In England, GCSE and A-level papers are overwhelmingly handwritten, and the ability to write legibly at pace for two or three hours is not a trivial skill. A student whose hand cramps after twenty minutes, or whose script is so slow that she cannot finish her argument, is penalised by a test that supposedly measures something else. Examiners regularly complain about illegible scripts. Fluent joined writing is, for most children, the quickest route to a hand that is both fast and readable. Telling children that handwriting does not matter, and then asking them to produce six thousand handwritten words under timed conditions, is a strange kind of kindness.

There is also a question of equality. Wealthy families will buy laptops, tutors and extra practice. They will also, in many cases, insist on good handwriting at home. If schools abandon the teaching of a skill because it is difficult and unfashionable, the children who suffer most are those who would have learned it only in the classroom. The gap does not close when we stop teaching something. It opens. A child who arrives at secondary school with a laboured, illegible hand and no systematic instruction behind it has been failed, however modern the decision that failed her might have sounded.

Then comes the argument people find embarrassing to make, because it sounds sentimental, but I think it deserves a hearing. Handwriting is a form of access to the written past. Birth certificates, wartime letters, a grandparent's recipe book, the marginal notes in a family Bible: much of the record of ordinary lives is in joined-up script. A generation that cannot read cursive cannot read those documents. Archivists already report this problem. In the United States, some historians have noted that students struggle with primary sources written in longhand, and volunteer transcribers are in demand for that reason. Teaching children to read cursive, and the surest way to teach reading it is to teach writing it, keeps a door open that would otherwise quietly close. It is a small door. But it leads to a lot of rooms.

I would not pretend that the opposing view is foolish. A serious critic might say that all this overstates the benefit, that print is perfectly legible and fast enough for most people, and that the hours spent on loops and joins could go to reading, grammar or digital literacy. These are fair points. The research on cursive versus print specifically is thinner than advocates tend to admit. Many adults, including highly literate ones, write in a hybrid of print and joined letters that no school ever taught them. A pragmatist could say that children will find their own style anyway, so why impose one?

The answer is that they will find their own style on top of a foundation, or they will not have one. Most adult handwriting is, in a sense, a personal deformation of what was learned in school. Remove the school model and there is nothing to deform. And the time cost is smaller than critics suggest. Good handwriting instruction takes short, regular sessions of ten or fifteen minutes, not hours. It can be woven into spelling practice, where joined letter patterns help children feel the shape of common endings such as "-ing" or "-tion". That is a genuine benefit, and one that proponents often neglect. Spelling is partly muscle memory, and a joined sequence of letters is easier to remember as a movement than as a list.

What should change is the manner of teaching. Too many schools treat handwriting as a matter of neatness, with gold stars for tidiness and red pen for sloppiness. That is the wrong emphasis. The goal is fluency: a hand that is automatic enough that the child can stop thinking about her letters and think about her ideas. Teachers should model the movements, let children practise in short bursts, and move on once the skill is secure, rather than dragging it out for years. They should also be honest that the endpoint is a personal, legible, reasonably quick hand, not a copperplate showpiece. Children who find joining unnatural should be allowed a simpler hybrid. Rigid dogma helps nobody.

Nor does any of this mean abandoning keyboards. A well-run primary school can teach both, and should. Typing lessons from around age nine or ten, handwriting from the start. The two skills do different jobs. One lets a child produce long, edited text efficiently. The other lets her think on paper, sit an exam, annotate a book, scribble a note, and read the writing of people who came before her.

The people who want to drop joined-up handwriting are responding to a real change in the world, and I sympathise. But the right response to a new tool is not to discard the old one as soon as it becomes inconvenient. It is to ask what the old skill still does that the new one cannot. In this case the answer is a good deal: it supports early reading, helps children who struggle with letter reversals, speeds up exam writing, narrows rather than widens the gap between rich and poor, and keeps the handwritten record legible. That is a long list for something that costs a few minutes a day.

Primary schools should keep teaching it. Keep it short, keep it practical, and keep it joined.
